title: Where were you yesterday?
title_target: გუშინ სად იყავი? — Gushin sad iq'avi?
goal: Talk about what has happened — and meet the most distinctive thing about Georgian: the subject changes its ending as soon as the story moves into the past.
bekal: use the past forms of the ten most common verbs
name past times: yesterday, last night, last week
put the -მა ending on the subject in past-tense sentences
understand when the -მა ending is NOT used

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — A long Saturday
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. Nino wants to know where Ani disappeared to last weekend. The whole dialogue is in the past — and one small letter at the end of a person's name holds the whole lesson of this unit.

lines.speaker: ნინო:
lines.id: Where were you yesterday? I called you three times.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Sorry! I was in Mtskheta, with Levan.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: We took a marshrutka. The trip took half an hour.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: We saw Svetitskhoveli. Levan explained everything.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: At a small restaurant. We ate khinkali and drank wine.
lines.literal: small — restaurant-in. khinkali — we-ate — and — wine — we-drank.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Levan, of course. I said "I'll pay," but he wouldn't agree.
lines.literal: Levan-(subject), what — saying — need. I — I-said "I — will-pay", but — not — he-agreed-with-me.

lines.speaker: ნინო:
lines.id: Ha, that's Levan for you. What did you do in the evening?
lines.literal: ha, this — Levan-is. evening-at — what — you-did?

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: We went back to Tbilisi and I went to bed early. I was so tired.
lines.literal: Tbilisi-in — we-returned — and — early — I-slept. very — I-got-tired.

notes: ⚠️ **This is the most distinctive thing about Georgian, and no other major language does it quite this way: in a past-tense sentence with an object, the subject takes the ending -მა.** ლევან**მა** ამიხსნა (Levan explained), დედა**მ** თქვა (Mom said), ანი**მ** იყიდა (Ani bought). In the present the ending doesn't change: *ლევანი ხსნის* (Levan explains).

**But -მა is NOT used with verbs that have no object.** *ლევანი წავიდა* (Levan left) — no -მა, because "leave" doesn't act on anything. Compare: *ლევანმა ღვინო იყიდა* (Levan bought wine) — there's an object, so -მა is used. The rule: **something is acted on → the subject takes -მა**.

**The pronouns მე, შენ, ჩვენ, თქვენ never change.** Only names and nouns change their ending. So *მე ვიყიდე* (I bought) looks the same as always, which means you can talk about yourself without touching this issue at all.

**The past forms of most verbs have prefixes you can't guess.** ვჭამ → **ვჭამე**, ვსვამ → **დავლიე**, ვხედავ → **ვნახე**, ვწერ → **დავწერე**, მივდივარ → **წავედი**, მოვდივარ → **მოვედი**. What stays the same is the ending: **-ე** for "I", **-ეთ** for "we", **-ა** for "he/she".

**იყავი / ვიყავი — the past of "to be".** ვიყავი (I was), იყავი (you were), იყო (he/she was), ვიყავით (we were), იყავით (you all were), იყვნენ (they were). This verb is used far too often to put off; learn all six.
**სამჯერ = three times.** The **-ჯერ** ending from unit 9: ერთჯერ, ორჯერ, სამჯერ, ბევრჯერ (many times).

**სვეტიცხოველი (Svetitskhoveli) in Mtskheta is an 11th-century cathedral** and one of the most important places for Georgians — according to tradition, Christ's robe is buried there. Mtskheta is half an hour from Tbilisi and is almost always the first trip offered to guests.

grammars.title: The past: ten verbs that cover almost every story
after: Look at the endings: **-ე** (I), **no ending** (you), **-ა** (he/she), **-ეთ** (we/you all). Only the prefixes change, and those really do have to be learned verb by verb.
For "they", the ending is **-ეს**: ჭამ**ეს** (they ate), ნახ**ეს** (they saw), წავიდ**ნენ** (they went).

grammars.title: The -მა ending: when to use it, when not to
body: One question settles the whole decision: **does the action act on something?**
after: For nouns ending in **-ი**, the ending is **-მა**: ლევან**ი** → ლევან**მა**. For those ending in **-ა**, just **-მ**: დედ**ა** → დედა**მ**, ანი → ანი**მ**.

⚠️ Don't panic if you get it wrong. Georgians understand you perfectly if you forget the -მა; even Georgian children take a while to lock this in. What matters is knowing the form exists and recognizing it when you hear it.

sections.title: Past time, and how to ask about it

blocks.title: Five questions about what's already happened
items: **გუშინ სად იყავი?** — Where were you yesterday?
**რა ქენი?** (ra keni) — What did you do?

blocks.text: The most useful exercise after this unit isn't going over the tables again, but telling the story of **your own yesterday** in five sentences. Use the verbs already in the table; don't hunt for new ones: *გუშინ სახლში ვიყავი. ქართული ვისწავლე. საღამოს ხინკალი ვჭამე. მეგობარი ვნახე. ადრე დავიძინე.* Those five sentences are already a complete story, built entirely from material you have.

⚠️ One thing that often makes beginners give up on this page: Georgian past forms look like a collection of unrelated words (ვსვამ → დავლიე?!). That's true, and there's no point pretending there's a pattern. But notice that the list you actually need is short — the ten verbs in the table above cover nearly everything people say about their day. Learn those ten, and let the rest come later.

vocab.en: I slept, I went to bed

exercises.prompt: Change into the past form for "I".
Add -მა to the subject if the sentence has an object; if not, leave the dictionary form.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: ვჭამე — ვნახე — წავედი — ვიყიდე — ვიყავი — ვისწავლე
გუშინ სად იყავი? — მცხეთაში ვიყავი. — ხინკალი ვჭამეთ. — ვინ იყიდა ღვინო? — ადრე დავიძინე.
გუშინ სად იყავი? — მცხეთაში ვიყავი. — მარშრუტკით წავედით. — ხინკალი ვჭამეთ. — ღვინო ლევანმა იყიდა. — ადრე დავიძინე.
wave: This is the hardest unit in the whole book. Don't rush on to unit 18 — do the exercises twice with a day in between, and tell the story of your yesterday out loud before you move on.
